content.text:
All 22 green. Now the systematic evaluation.

**Step 1 — Naming evaluation (first priority).** I walked every name in the file. `runScenario`, `quotePremium`, `policyBasePremiumOf`, `sumOfRateAmounts`, `ratesForItem`, `ratesForPolicy`, `holdsAnEarlierQuote`, `isLongStanding` — all read as domain language and match what they do. One candidate stood out:

`toSubunits` / `SUBUNITS_PER_G` are generic money-plumbing names, but they are used in three places against a documented invariant ("money is carried in hundredths of a G"), and renaming to e.g. `toHundredthsOfG` would only restate the constant. Not an improvement, just churn.

**Step 2 — the one real finding.** `sumOfItemModifierAmounts` reaches for `basePremiumOf(item)`, but `policyBasePremiumOf` deliberately does *not* use raw base premiums for components — it prices blocks. So the two functions disagree about what an item's base premium is, and the disagreement is silent. Today nothing catches it: no passing test has a cursed component inside a block of three. The `moonstone, cursed: true` test has a single moonstone, where block pricing is a no-op.

That is a latent bug, not a refactoring — and fixing it means choosing a rule the spec has not yet been asked to settle (does a curse on one moonstone of a block surcharge 50% of 25, or of the 60-block?). Deciding it now would be implementing ahead. I left it alone and did not add a test. Flagging it for whoever writes that example.

**Step 3 — Rules 3 and 4.** No duplication found: `sumOfBasePremiums`, `partition`, `groupByType` are each used at a single conceptual site but are the extraction that makes `policyBasePremiumOf` readable. No dead elements; every constant and helper is reachable from `runScenario`.

**Step 4 — the refactoring I applied.** `groupByType` was the one function whose implementation was heavier than its intent:

```ts
for (const item of items) groups.set(item.type, [...(groups.get(item.type) ?? []), item]);
```

Per item this rebuilds the whole accumulated array with a spread — quadratic in group size, and the reader has to decode the spread-plus-nullish-coalescing to see that it means "append". I changed it to push into the existing array.

**APP mass, `groupByType` body:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| constants | 0 | 0 |
| bindings | 5 (`groups`, `items`, `item`×3) | 5 |
| invocations | 4 → 8 (`Map`, `set`, `get`, spread-copy) | 4 → 8 (`Map`, `get`, `push`, `set`... ) |
| conditionals | 1 → 4 (`??`) | 1 → 4 (`??`) |
| loops | 1 → 5 | 1 → 5 |
| assignments | 0 | 1 → 6 (`groups.set` on miss only) |

Mass before **22**, after **23**. Mass went *up* by 1 — and I kept the change anyway. This is Rule 2 trumping APP, exactly as the priority order requires: the new body says "get the group, append to it" in the order a reader thinks it, and the accidental O(n²) copy is gone. A one-point mass increase for a genuine clarity and complexity win is the right trade.

Tests re-run after the change: 22 passed, 24 todo, all green.

**One correction to your framing.** You told me the newcomer's-cursed-sword integration test is "genuinely redundant in coverage terms" with the earlier curse-surcharge test. I checked both rather than taking it on faith, and it holds — line 145 and line 299 have byte-identical inputs and the same expectation of 165. So the note is accurate, and deduplication was correctly out of scope. I mention it only because I verified it rather than assuming.

Regarding what's next: the second integration example (cursed enchantment-7 sword, 3 years, second quote) should pass on arrival too. Tracing it: 100 base + 50 curse + 30 high-ench + 10 first-insurance − 20 loyalty − 15 follow-up + 5 fee = 160. Every one of those five modifiers already has a passing test, and `ratesForPolicy` already composes them additively. Expect a second no-op Green — worth predicting explicitly in the Red phase so a surprise pass isn't mistaken for a correct one.
